A user thanked Appwrite, saying its Discord community is very helpful and its self-hosting guide is great. They contrasted this with a 'terrible experience' with Supabase, which they felt was crippling its self-hosted option.
One commenter said Supabase's self-hosted option was 'wack' when they tried it a few months earlier. After reading the comparison in the thread, they said they might give Appwrite a try.

A user pointed to Appwrite's installation and production docs as a model and said they would love something similar from Supabase. A Supabase representative replied that 'the appwrite docs here are very nice' and said Supabase would improve its own self-hosting docs.
A returning user said they kicked the tires on Appwrite a year earlier and liked it but didn't have a big need for it then. They noted that a lot of great features had been added since.

A developer evaluating Firebase and Supabase for a new project was about to give up and go back to Laravel, but found Appwrite 'very interesting'. Their first question was whether Postgres is supported; the team replied that it was not yet supported.

A user said they weren't the target market because the point of a BaaS for them is not having to maintain infrastructure, and self-hosted Appwrite still requires that. They also asked for an always-on container compute model, arguing functions have mainly downsides for non-hobby projects.

A critic raised several concerns: Appwrite is written in PHP, which they doubted for extensibility and scalability; it had no Cloud version yet, so it wasn't ready 'as a service'; and it isn't built on Postgres. They also said GraphQL progress was slow and felt the project moved slower than Supabase on features they care about.

A user who had watched Supabase for months without adopting it said they were 'instantly sold' on Appwrite. They said they can easily install it for home projects, unlike Supabase, and would pay for Appwrite's hosted option for commercial apps.

Skeptic: running Appwrite on your own DigitalOcean droplet means it isn't really a BaaS anymore. They called 'self-host your own BAAS' an oxymoron, since developers who choose Firebase don't want to manage servers.
A user said they couldn't find docs on scaling. They asked how Appwrite scales its WebSocket connection pool, workers and cloud functions.

A self-described wary user said the product looks awesome and they would think of a project to try it on. They added that the polish and content of the website really helped and left them very impressed.
A commenter noted this was the first 'Firebase clone' they had seen that attempts to implement the Firestore database model, and called it neat.

An early tester liked that Appwrite provides a containerized setup for offline development. They had found the offline dev story lacking in another service they tried, and said containers should make distributed dev and testing much easier.

Early users said Appwrite was exactly what they were looking for but complained there was little information on architecture and the tech stack. They specifically wanted details on the database backend, how to back it up, how it scales and the roadmap; one said a quick search turned up nothing.

A non-affiliated long-time follower called BaaS a crowded, tough segment. They said Appwrite's opinionated abstractions become limiting once you want flexibility or scale, but welcomed it as an open-source option that keeps Supabase honest.

Several commenters complained that the Appwrite Sites launch thread was flooded with undisclosed employee or bot praise and called it 'the most overly positive and least critical HN submission'. One said the comment spam was a footgun, because the product itself looks worthwhile as an open-source alternative to Vercel.

An Android developer was excited by the 1.0 release and especially by the planned push notifications. They asked how close Appwrite's front-end API is to Firebase's, citing the learning curve of migrating an existing Firebase app.
